issues.legal_issue: A pure question of law based on admitted or undisputed facts may be raised for the first time during an appeal when refusing permission to raise it would not be justified by waiver or prejudice to the opposing party.
material_facts: The appellant did not include the objection concerning the permissible period for mesne profits in the memorandum of appeal and first sought to raise it when the appeal was argued.
The objection presented a question of law that did not depend on resolving disputed facts.
The parties had not previously disputed the permissible period, so the appellant’s silence did not amount to a concession or election on that question.
The respondent could not have been prejudiced by the late objection because a separate claim for the relevant mesne profits was already time-barred.
issues.conclusion: By majority, the High Court was wrong to refuse permission to raise the additional ground; the appellant was entitled to urge it in the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: An appellate court has discretion to permit an additional ground, but a pure question of law resting on admitted or proved undisputed facts may be raised at a later stage, including in a final appeal. The refusal of permission may be interfered with when it disregards that principle. The Court relied on Wilson v. United Counties Bank Ltd., Yeswant Deorao Deshmukh v. Walchand Ramchand Kothari, M. K. Ranganathan v. Government of Madras, Ittyavira Mathai v. Varkey Varkey and Rehmat-un-Nissa Begam v. Price; it distinguished a mixed question of law and fact.

rule.if: appeal_from_final_decree and pure_question_of_law and facts_admitted_or_undisputed and opponent_not_prejudiced

predicates.appeal_from_final_decree: A party appealed from a final decree and sought to raise an additional ground during the appeal.
predicates.pure_question_of_law: The additional ground raised a question of law rather than a question requiring factual determination.
predicates.facts_admitted_or_undisputed: The facts needed to decide the additional ground were admitted or established without controversy.
predicates.opponent_not_prejudiced: Allowing the additional ground would not impair the opposing party’s ability to meet it or deprive that party of an available claim.

issues.definition: When a party appealing a final decree raises a pure legal ground based on undisputed facts and the opposing party would not be prejudiced, the ground must be permitted despite its lateness.

issues.legal_issue: A direction for an inquiry into future mesne profits in a possession suit is governed by the statutory outer limit even if the direction is expressed as continuing until delivery of possession.
material_facts: A preliminary decree in a suit for possession and mesne profits directed an inquiry into future mesne profits from the institution of the suit until delivery of possession.
Possession of some of the properties was delivered more than three years after the preliminary decree.
The final decree included mesne profits for a period extending beyond three years from the preliminary decree.
The majority construed the preliminary direction consistently with the governing rule rather than as authorizing recovery beyond its limit.
issues.conclusion: By majority, the decree-holder could not recover future mesne profits for a period beyond the three-year limit running from the preliminary decree.
issues.legal_principle: Order XX, rule 12(1)(c) of the Code of Civil Procedure directs an inquiry into future mesne profits until the first of the specified terminating events, including the expiration of three years from the decree; rule 12(2) provides for a final decree based on the inquiry. A direction that does not set out all the alternatives is construed in conformity with the rule. The Court relied on Girish Chunder Lahiri v. Shoshi Shikhareswar Roy and the line of cases applying that construction, including Venkata Kumara v. Subbayamma, Uttamram v. Kishordas, Trailokya v. Jogendra, Godayarti Raja v. Ramachandraswami, Narayan v. Sono, Kunwar Jagdish Chandra v. Bulaqi Das and Kanai Lal v. Shyam Kishore.

predicates.suit_for_possession_and_mesne_profits: A claimant brought a proceeding seeking possession of immovable property and mesne profits.
predicates.future_profit_inquiry_ordered: The court directed an inquiry into mesne profits accruing after the proceeding began.
predicates.possession_not_delivered_within_outer_li: The person entitled to possession did not receive it before the legally prescribed outer limit for the future-profit inquiry.

issues.definition: When a possession-and-mesne-profits proceeding includes an inquiry into future profits and possession is not delivered within the legally prescribed outer limit, recovery of those future profits is confined by that limit.

issues.legal_issue: An unappealed preliminary direction for an inquiry into future mesne profits does not bar a challenge at the final-decree stage to the permissible period when the direction did not decide a controversy between the parties.
material_facts: The preliminary decree directed an inquiry into future mesne profits until delivery of possession but did not resolve a dispute between the parties about the legally permissible duration of that inquiry.
No party had raised or contested the duration question when the preliminary decree was made.
The appellant challenged the duration when appealing from the final decree.
The majority held that the proper period became material for decision when the final decree was made and that the preliminary direction was not an adjudication of that issue.
issues.conclusion: By majority, the appellant was not precluded from challenging the period of mesne profits; section 97 of the Code of Civil Procedure and res judicata did not bar the challenge.
issues.legal_principle: Section 97 of the Code of Civil Procedure precludes a challenge to a preliminary decree’s correctness in an appeal from the final decree where the preliminary decree adjudicated the matter in issue. The majority held that a direction under Order XX, rule 12(1)(c) for an inquiry into future mesne profits is an exercise of statutory discretion, not an adjudication of a controversy about the ultimate period of entitlement. Because that question is determined when the final decree is made, the direction did not operate as res judicata under section 11 or general principles. The dissent considered the unappealed direction final and binding.

predicates.appeal_from_final_decree: A party appealed from a final decree following an earlier preliminary decree.
predicates.preliminary_decree_directed_future_profi: The preliminary decree directed an inquiry into mesne profits accruing after the proceeding began.
predicates.no_duration_dispute_adjudicated: The parties did not contest, and the preliminary decree did not decide, the permissible duration of the future-profit award.

issues.definition: A party appealing from a final decree may challenge the duration of future mesne profits when the preliminary decree directed an inquiry but did not adjudicate a dispute about that duration.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court may not enhance an award of mesne profits without adequately explaining why the trial court’s assessment should be disturbed.
material_facts: The trial court assessed mesne profits after considering a commissioner’s report and the evidence concerning the properties and relevant periods.
The High Court substantially increased the rates for several items without adequately explaining why the trial court’s findings were wrong.
In assessing the rates, the High Court overlooked the period of economic depression and, for one item, awarded more than the claimant had sought.
The Supreme Court could not determine the proper quantum from the High Court’s reasons and sent the matter back for fresh assessment.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s assessment was set aside, and the matter was remanded for the quantum of mesne profits to be determined afresh, subject to the permissible period fixed by the majority.
issues.legal_principle: An appellate court varying a trial court’s assessment of mesne profits must engage with the trial court’s findings and the evidentiary basis for the assessment and give reasons for the variation. The High Court’s unexplained increases, failure to account for relevant economic conditions, and award exceeding the claim did not support its assessment. The reassessment was confined to the period permitted under Order XX, rule 12(1)(c) of the Code of Civil Procedure.

predicates.appeal_concerns_mesne_profit_quantum: The appeal concerns the amount of mesne profits awarded by the trial court.
predicates.appellate_court_increases_trial_assessme: The appellate court increases the trial court’s assessment of mesne profits.
predicates.increase_lacks_reasoned_support: The appellate court does not adequately explain its disagreement with the trial court’s findings or address material evidence relevant to the amount.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns mesne profits and the appellate court raises the trial assessment without adequate reasons or engagement with material evidence, the enhanced assessment must be set aside for reassessment.
